query: For W–Cu metal-matrix composites used in heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications, what single intervention could increase thermal conductivity while retaining mechanical durability and irradiation resistance? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an otherwise comparable W–Cu composite, defines the application conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Performing liquid-metal dealloying on the as-cast WTaVTi precursor by immersing it in molten Cu at 1200 °C for 96 h will form a bicontinuous, directionally aligned composite structure with Cu channels and RHEA ligaments bonded by a W-rich interlayer. This engineered microstructure will enhance thermal conductivity (especially at high temperature) while maintaining mechanical durability and resistance to low-energy He+ irradiation compared to unprocessed W–Cu composites or pure W.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast, nominally equiatomic WTaVTi refractory high-entropy alloy with a directionally solidified dendrite–interdendrite structure (W/Ta-rich dendrites and Ti/V-rich interdendritic channels).
generation.intervention: Liquid-metal dealloying by immersion in molten Cu at 1200 °C for 96 h, which selectively extracts Ti from the interdendritic regions to form nearly pure FCC Cu channels and leaves behind immiscible W, Ta, and V forming BCC RHEA ligaments.
generation.conditions: The processing is carried out in a vacuum-sealed silica environment at 1200 °C for 96 h, with subsequent evaluations of thermal conductivity from room temperature to ~800 °C (and extrapolated above 1000 °C) and He+ irradiation screening at 25 keV up to blistering fluences near 8–8.5 × 10^17 atoms cm−2.
generation.structural_mediator: The resulting bicontinuous structure composed of approximately 63.6 vol.% BCC RHEA ligaments and 36.4 vol.% nearly pure FCC Cu channels, with a spontaneously formed ~300 nm W-rich passivating interlayer at the RHEA/Cu interfaces.
generation.mechanism: During dealloying, Ti (which has a negative heat of mixing with Cu) preferentially exchanges with Cu and dissolves, forming Cu channels, while the immiscible metals (W, Ta, V) remain as stable RHEA ligaments. The subsequent formation of a W‐rich interlayer—due to the strong positive heat of mixing between W and Cu—passivates the interface to arrest further exchange, ensuring strong interfacial bonding. The aligned Cu channels serve as efficient thermal conduits, while the complex RHEA lattice resists He-induced swelling.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified composite will exhibit a substantial increase in thermal conductivity (especially at temperatures above ~650 °C) relative to the unprocessed WTaVTi precursor and pure W, while also showing lower He-induced swelling and delayed blister formation under irradiation. The overall mechanical durability is expected to remain high due to the robust, continuous RHEA network.
generation.baseline: The baseline comparisons include the unprocessed WTaVTi precursor, pure W, pure Cu, and conventional W–Cu composites. The irradiation behavior is compared with pure W and other related compositions such as WTa and WTaV.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold under the specific processing conditions of vacuum-sealed exposure to molten Cu at 1200 °C for 96 h and for temperature-dependent thermal conductivity measurements in the range of room temperature to at least 800 °C (with high-temperature performance extrapolated above 1000 °C). Its validity for irradiation is restricted to low-energy (25 keV) He+ implantation scenarios and may not extend to neutron irradiation or other types of radiation damage.
generation.uncertainty: While the evidence supports improved thermal conductivity and irradiation resistance in this system, quantitative values of these enhancements and the exact impact on mechanical strength remain uncertain and require further experimental determination.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples of the as-cast WTaVTi alloy and subject a set to liquid-metal dealloying by immersion in molten Cu under the specified conditions (1200 °C for 96 h) in a vacuum-sealed silica environment. Characterize the microstructure using SEM, TEM, and EDS to confirm formation of Cu channels, RHEA ligaments, and the W-rich interlayer. Measure temperature-dependent thermal conductivity (using laser-flash analysis) from room temperature up to ~800 °C, and subject samples to 25 keV He+ irradiation while monitoring swelling and blistering via AFM. Evaluate mechanical properties with nanoindentation.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (SEM/TEM/EDS) to verify the formation of the bicontinuous structure and the W-rich interlayer
AFM measurements of swelling and blistering onset under 25 keV He+ irradiation
Nanoindentation tests to assess hardness and mechanical durability
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the dealloyed composite does not exhibit a significantly higher thermal conductivity (particularly above ~650 °C) relative to the baseline materials, or if it shows similar or worse He+-induced swelling and blistering compared to pure W or conventional W–Cu composites, then the hypothesis will be rejected.
